title: A theme before the Louvre Virgin of the Rocks
target: Virgin of the Rocks · Louvre version
documented: The Met identifies a shared investigation of the kneeling Virgin and children, while associating this sheet more closely with a lost design known through contemporary copies.
looking: Compare the inclination of the Virgin and the intervals around the children. Look for a developing problem of protection and encounter rather than an exact outline waiting to be painted.
limit: This is not securely identified as a direct preparatory sheet for the surviving Louvre panel. Similar subject matter alone would not establish that relationship.

title: One investigation, two surviving versions
target: Virgin of the Rocks · National Gallery, London
documented: The Met discusses the sheet in relation to the theme of both surviving Virgin of the Rocks paintings. The London painting must be distinguished from the Louvre version.
looking: Open the National Gallery record beside the sheet. Consider how enclosing rock, suspended gestures and the placement of children turn a kneeling encounter into a coherent environment.
limit: The sheet does not document a complete sequence from first drawing through both panels. The lost intermediate design discussed by the Met remains missing.

title: From a head study to a family group
target: Virgin and Child with Saint Anne · Musée du Louvre
documented: Carmen C. Bambach’s Met account connects this head study to the final design of the Louvre painting, while discussing disagreement over the drawing’s authorship and technical evidence.
looking: Follow the face into its surrounding hair and veil, then consider how a bowed head participates in a larger chain of attention. Soft transitions are structural choices, not simply a lack of finish.
limit: The Met’s attribution argument is a named scholarly position. A screen reproduction cannot substitute for examination of the chalk layers, and it cannot settle every stage of the painting’s development.

title: A studio body becomes a monumental seer
documented: The Met identifies the sheet as studies from a young male studio model for the monumental female Libyan Sibyl. The figure in the fresco is clothed except at the shoulders and arms.
looking: Compare the turn of the torso with the separate investigations of foot and head. Ask what the painted book, drapery and elevated architectural seat add to the bodily action.
limit: The drawing is much smaller than the painted figure. It records selected investigations rather than every intervening drawing or a single uninterrupted performance.

title: An intimate group tested in red chalk
target: Madonna in the Meadow · Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna
documented: The Met identifies the central composition and the smaller arm and drapery studies with the Vienna painting. Its account places this sheet late among the surviving preparatory drawings.
looking: Track the children’s reaching arms and the Virgin’s enclosing body. Separate the central arrangement from the small marginal studies: a page can hold related decisions without becoming one scene.
limit: The Met discusses evidence for a final cartoon that has not survived. That absent transfer drawing must not be supplied by a speculative digital reconstruction.

title: A model study enters a workshop composition
target: Holy Family with the Infant Saint John · Vienna version
relationship: Preparation for a composition executed with assistants
documented: The Met connects the studies to a Holy Family composition known through painted versions in Vienna and Rome, largely executed by Raphael’s close assistants.
looking: Consider the child’s reaching movement as a link between people. Compare isolated weight and gesture on paper with the task of connecting a child on a lap to another figure.
limit: Do not describe the surviving painting as entirely executed by Raphael on the strength of this drawing. The institutional account distinguishes invention from workshop execution.

title: A shared design does not erase version differences
target: Holy Family with the Infant Saint John · Rome version
documented: The Met names a painted version in the Galleria Borghese alongside the Vienna version. Both belong to the documented afterlife of the composition studied on this sheet.
looking: Use the two institutional images to ask where a shared pose becomes a different pictorial encounter. Attend to the child’s reach, surrounding figures and the spacing that connects them.
limit: This pairing does not establish a precise order between the two paintings or assign every passage to a named assistant. Those are separate attribution questions.

title: A drawing made after a painting, through a print
relationship: Later reinterpretation through a reproductive print
documented: The Met describes Rembrandt’s drawing as based on an early print after Leonardo’s mural. It emphasizes changes to the figures and the compression of space.
looking: Compare how reactions travel along the table. Follow changes in the grouping and intensity of gestures rather than testing whether Rembrandt copied every detail faithfully.
limit: Rembrandt did not make this drawing as a preparatory study for Leonardo’s mural or necessarily from direct sight of it. The print is an important intervening object.

title: A figure revised across several sheets
target: Dancers at the Barre · The Phillips Collection
documented: The Met relates this tracing-paper figure and at least five other drawings to the Phillips painting. It identifies visible reworking rather than an entirely new invention in one sitting.
looking: Compare the angle of the back and raised leg with the barre. The supports and contours organize force and balance; they are not only anatomical description.
limit: The broad dating and family of variants do not yield a secure chronological order for every line or sheet. Bare charcoal is not evidence that the drawing was abandoned.

title: A design travels through engraving into painting
target: Lucretia · School of Raphael, Courtauld collection, P1966.GP.336
documented: The Met discusses a Courtauld painting attributed to the school of Raphael that follows Marcantonio Raimondi’s engraved Lucretia design. The drawing, print and painting are distinct objects.
looking: Compare the body’s turn with the changing treatment of the head and setting. A recognizable pose can travel while meaning, scale and authorship change.
limit: This is not presented as Raphael’s direct preparatory drawing for that painting. The relationship includes an intermediary engraving and a school attribution.

title: A kneeling child within a circular composition
target: The Alba Madonna · National Gallery of Art, Washington
documented: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen identifies its Study for the Kneeling Infant St John with Raphael’s Alba Madonna and compares it with a surviving composition drawing.
looking: Open the museum’s drawing and the completed painting. Follow the child’s kneeling support, turned head and relation to the cross within the larger circle.
limit: This source-only study is held outside our hosted paper selection. Use the museum’s reproduction; no new image reuse permission is assumed. A local catalog identifier has not been invented.

title: A pen study for a public altarpiece
target: Madonna del Pesce · Museo Nacional del Prado
documented: The National Galleries of Scotland identifies its drawing as preparation for the Prado painting, made as an altarpiece for San Domenico in Naples.
looking: Look first at the movement of the whole group rather than isolated finish. Compare the rhythm of gestures and the distribution of standing and seated figures with the altarpiece.
limit: The museum provides its drawing image under a personal-use license. We link to its record instead of copying it into a public deployment. The image’s finish alone cannot establish its exact place in every surviving study.

title: A study is enlarged into another work on paper
documented: The Met identifies the violinist sheet as an intermediate pastel study, squared for transfer, for The Dance Lesson. The final work is pastel and black chalk on joined papers, not an oil painting.
looking: Trace the musician’s bodily support and instrument, then examine how the surrounding dancer and barre establish a shared room. A grid organizes transfer but does not explain every adjustment.
limit: A useful study-to-finished-work comparison need not be drawing-to-oil. Do not erase the material identity of the final pastel to fit a simpler story.

title: A proposal is not the monument as built
target: Tomb of Julius II · San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome
documented: Bambach’s Met account discusses the early tomb design, its attribution history and the much reduced monument installed in 1545. The drawing’s precise construction also served a demonstration function.
looking: Move between the measured architectural framework and the figures occupying it. Ask how viewing a proposal differs from moving around an installed monument.
limit: The final structure is not a literal realization of this sheet. Its changing location, scale and program matter; the drawing’s disputed authorship is retained.

title: An independent drawing becomes a circulating design
documented: The Met’s discussion distinguishes Raphael’s independent drawing from Raimondi’s later engraved designs and notes their substantial differences in scale and head design.
looking: Follow the contour and drapery through both objects. The same-direction relationship requires care: transfer to a printing plate is not a simple photograph of a drawing.
limit: Do not present Vasari’s later account as a contemporary contract or assume that every drawing resembling a print was designed expressly for that print.
